title: Αἰθίοψ
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 11 (= Perry 393). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Αἰθίοπά τις ὠνήσατο τοιοῦτον αὐτῷ τὸ χρῶμα εἶναι δοκῶν ἀμελείᾳ τοῦ πρότερον ἔχοντος.
sentences.tr: Aithiopa tis ōnēsato toiouton autōi to chrōma einai dokōn ameleiāi tou proteron echontos.
sentences.l: Someone bought an Ethiopian, thinking his colour to be such by the neglect of the man having him before.
sentences.i: A man bought an Ethiopian, supposing his colour to be as it was through the carelessness of his former owner.
sentences.n: Αἰθίοψ is the ordinary Greek word for a black African, and it is transparent: αἴθω “burn” + ὤψ “face”, the burnt-faced man. δοκῶν, “thinking”, takes an accusative and infinitive for what is thought (τὸ χρῶμα … εἶναι). ἀμελείᾳ is a bare dative of cause, “by neglect”. τοῦ πρότερον ἔχοντος is an articular participle used as a noun — “of the one having him before”, i.e. the previous owner; Greek makes nouns out of participles far more freely than English, and you will see it constantly.

sentences.t: Καὶ παραλαβὼν οἴκαδε, πάντα μὲν αὐτῷ προσῆγε τὰ ῥύμματα, πᾶσι δὲ λούτροις ἐπειρᾶτο καθαίρειν.
sentences.tr: Kai paralabōn oikade, panta men autōi prosēge ta rhymmata, pasi de loutrois epeirato kathairein.
sentences.l: And having taken him home, all the soaps he applied to him, and with all baths he tried to cleanse him.
sentences.i: He took him home, applied every soap there was to him, and tried to scour him clean with bath after bath.
sentences.n: μέν … δέ sets the two attempts side by side — soaps on the one hand, baths on the other; the pair is a signpost, not two separate claims. A ῥύμμα is anything used for scouring: soap, lye, fuller's earth. προσῆγε and ἐπειρᾶτο are imperfects of attempt — he kept applying, kept trying.

sentences.t: Καὶ τὸ μὲν χρῶμα μεταβάλλειν οὐκ εἶχε, νοσεῖν δὲ τῷ πονεῖν παρεσκεύασεν.
sentences.tr: Kai to men chrōma metaballein ouk eiche, nosein de tōi ponein pareskeuasen.
sentences.l: And the colour he had no power to change, but to fall sick he brought about by the labouring.
sentences.i: The colour he had no power to change; what he did bring about, by all that labour, was to make the man ill.
sentences.n: ἔχω with an infinitive means “be able”, not “have” — οὐκ εἶχε μεταβάλλειν, “he could not change it”. τῷ πονεῖν is an articular infinitive in the dative of means, “by the toiling”: put the article in front of any infinitive and it becomes a noun that can take a case. A second μέν … δέ, this one setting what he could not do against what he did.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι μένουσιν αἱ φύσεις ὡς προῆλθον τὴν ἀρχήν.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti menousin hai physeis hōs proēlthon tēn archēn.
sentences.l: The fable shows that natures remain as they came forth at the outset.
sentences.n: The house formula ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι, “the fable shows that…”, which closes most of these pieces. τὴν ἀρχήν is an adverbial accusative, “at the outset”. μένουσιν is a present of general truth; προῆλθον looks back to the one moment of origin.
